children.title: DNA, RNA & Protein Synthesis
children.description: How base pairing, transcription, translation, and the codon code turn genes into proteins — and how gene expression and mutations shape cells.

children.title: Complementary Base Pairing
children.description: Which bases pair with which, and how DNA and RNA differ.

teach.headline: A Pairs With T, G Pairs With C
teach.body:
In DNA the bases pair in fixed partners: **adenine (A) with thymine (T)** and **guanine (G) with cytosine (C)**. Because the pairing is fixed, each strand is a template for rebuilding the other.

RNA follows the same rule with one swap: it has no thymine, so **adenine pairs with uracil (U)**. This pairing is how DNA is copied and how mRNA is transcribed from a gene.
teach.mnemonic: A-T = APPLE TREE. G-C = GOOD CALL. In RNA, T retires and URACIL pairs with A.
teach.poweredIdea: DNA bases pair A-T and G-C; in RNA, adenine pairs with uracil instead of thymine.

data.prompt: In DNA, the base adenine (A) always pairs with _____.
In RNA, adenine pairs with _____ instead of thymine.

data.story: One strand of a DNA molecule reads T-A-C-G.
data.question: What is the base sequence of the complementary DNA strand?
options: A-T-G-C
T-A-C-G
U-A-G-C
A-U-G-C
data.explanation: Pair each base with its partner: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C gives A-T-G-C. (Uracil would only appear in RNA.)

achievement.flavor: You read one strand and write its complement, swapping in uracil whenever the strand is RNA.

children.title: Transcription & Translation
children.description: The DNA-to-RNA-to-protein pipeline and where each step happens.

teach.headline: DNA to RNA to Protein
teach.body:
The central dogma is **DNA → RNA → protein**.

**Transcription** copies a gene from DNA into messenger RNA inside the **nucleus**. The mRNA then travels out to a **ribosome**, where **translation** reads the mRNA codons and tRNA delivers the matching amino acids to build the protein.

![Labeled DNA double helix showing sugar-phosphate backbone and base pairs](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_dna_structure.svg)

figures.alt: DNA double helix with sugar-phosphate backbone and nitrogenous base pairs labeled
figures.caption: Genes are stored as DNA base sequences before transcription.

teach.mnemonic: TRANSCRIBE = WRITE mRNA in the NUCLEUS. TRANSLATE = READ it at the RIBOSOME.
teach.poweredIdea: Transcription (DNA to mRNA) happens in the nucleus; translation (mRNA to protein) happens at the ribosome.

data.prompt: Copying a gene from DNA into messenger RNA is called _____.
data.hint: Trans + write = copying DNA to mRNA

data.prompt: In the diagram, the alternating sugar-_____ chain forms the DNA backbone.

data.goal: Order the steps that turn a gene into a working protein.
data.initialState: Gene in the DNA of the nucleus

blocks.label: Transcribe gene into mRNA (in the nucleus)
blocks.narration: RNA polymerase copies the gene's DNA into messenger RNA.

blocks.label: mRNA exits the nucleus
blocks.narration: The mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm.

blocks.label: mRNA attaches to a ribosome
blocks.narration: The ribosome locks onto the mRNA to begin reading it.

blocks.label: Ribosome reads codons; tRNA brings amino acids
blocks.narration: Each codon pairs with a tRNA carrying the matching amino acid.

blocks.label: Polypeptide folds into a working protein
blocks.narration: The finished amino-acid chain folds into its functional shape.

data.poweredIdea: Gene expression is a pipeline: transcribe in the nucleus, then translate at the ribosome.

data.correct: Occurs at the ribosome (mRNA to protein)
distractors: Occurs in the nucleus (DNA to mRNA)

data.story: An antibiotic works by jamming the ribosomes of bacterial cells so they cannot operate.
data.question: Which process does the drug stop directly?
options: Translation (building proteins from mRNA)
Transcription (copying DNA into mRNA)
DNA replication
Base pairing within the DNA helix
data.explanation: Ribosomes are the site of translation, so blocking them halts protein synthesis.

achievement.flavor: You route a gene from nucleus to ribosome: transcribe to mRNA, then translate to protein.

children.title: Codons & the Genetic Code
children.description: Three bases at a time: how mRNA is read into amino acids.

teach.headline: Three Bases Code One Amino Acid
teach.body:
mRNA is read in groups of three bases called **codons**. Each codon specifies **one amino acid** (a few codons mean 'start' or 'stop').

A codon table converts each codon to its amino acid. At the ribosome, **tRNA** molecules carrying specific amino acids match the codons one by one, building the amino-acid chain that becomes a protein.
teach.mnemonic: CODON = 3-LETTER WORD = 1 AMINO ACID. Read mRNA three bases at a time.
teach.poweredIdea: Each codon is three mRNA bases that code for one amino acid.

data.prompt: A group of three consecutive mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid is a _____.

data.story: A test item asks about the meaning of three consecutive nucleotides in a gene.
data.question: What is the significance of three consecutive nucleotides?
data.answer: They code for one amino acid.
options: They code for one amino acid.
They code for three amino acids.
They code for one complete protein.
They code for three complete proteins.
data.explanation: Three bases form a single codon, which specifies exactly one amino acid.

data.story: A ribosome is actively translating an mRNA strand into a protein.
data.question: Which action is taking place at the ribosome?
data.answer: tRNA molecules carrying specific amino acids match the mRNA codons.
options: tRNA molecules carrying specific amino acids match the mRNA codons.
mRNA is being copied from one strand of the DNA helix.
A polypeptide is broken back down into amino acids and bases.
Single-stranded mRNA is converted into double-stranded tRNA.
data.explanation: During translation, each mRNA codon pairs with a tRNA carrying the matching amino acid.

data.correct: Brings amino acids to the ribosome
distractors: Carries the gene's message from the nucleus

achievement.flavor: You read mRNA three bases at a time, knowing each codon names exactly one amino acid.

children.title: Point vs Frameshift Mutations
children.description: How a one-base change differs from inserting or deleting a base.

teach.headline: One Base Off vs Everything Shifts
teach.body:
A **mutation** changes the DNA base sequence. A **point mutation** (substitution) swaps a single base for another, usually altering at most one codon — so at most one amino acid changes.

A **frameshift** mutation **inserts or deletes** a base. That shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is read in the wrong groups — usually a much larger change to the protein.
teach.mnemonic: POINT = SWAP ONE LETTER. FRAMESHIFT = ADD/DROP A LETTER → every later WORD is garbled.
teach.poweredIdea: A point mutation swaps one base; a frameshift inserts or deletes a base and shifts every later codon.

data.prompt: A mutation that inserts or deletes a base and shifts the reading frame is a _____ mutation.
data.hint: It shifts how codons are grouped

data.scenario: A point mutation in the hemoglobin gene swaps a single base in the second codon.
data.clinicalHook: Changing GAG to GTG swaps glutamic acid for valine — the change behind sickle cell trait.
data.poweredIdea: A single base substitution can change one amino acid and alter the whole protein's behavior.

data.scenario: Near the start of a gene, compare two mutations: (1) one base is swapped for a different base, and (2) one extra base is inserted.
data.predictPrompt: Which mutation more drastically changes the resulting protein?
predictOptions: The single-base swap, because it rewrites the whole protein
The inserted base, because it shifts the reading frame and garbles every codon after it
Both change exactly one amino acid, so they are equal
Neither one changes the protein at all
data.runNarrative: The swap changes at most the one codon it sits in — often a single amino acid. The insertion pushes every base after it into new codon groupings, so all downstream codons (and their amino acids) are read differently.
data.truthSummary: A substitution is local; a frameshift insertion or deletion shifts the reading frame and changes everything downstream.

bugCandidates.label: I assumed both mutations just change one amino acid
bugCandidates.explanation: A frameshift re-groups every downstream base into new codons, so far more than one amino acid changes.

bugCandidates.label: I thought a single-base swap rewrites the entire protein
bugCandidates.explanation: A substitution usually alters at most the one codon it lands in.

bugCandidates.label: I assumed mutations never affect the protein
bugCandidates.explanation: Some substitutions are silent, but inserting a base near the start clearly changes the protein.

data.poweredIdea: A frameshift shifts the reading frame, changing far more of the protein than a single-base swap.

data.correct: An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame
distractors: A single base swapped for another base
A mutation that is always harmless
A change only to the start codon

achievement.flavor: You weigh a one-base swap against an insertion and know which one garbles every codon downstream.

children.title: Gene Expression & Cancer
children.description: Same DNA, different genes switched on — and what happens when cell-cycle control is lost.

teach.headline: Same DNA, Different Genes Switched On
teach.body:
Every cell in an organism carries the **same DNA**. Cells differ because they **express** (switch on) different genes — proteins regulate which genes are active. This drives **differentiation**: a skin cell and a nerve cell read different pages of the same instruction book.

When the genes that **control the cell cycle** are damaged, a cell can divide without stopping. That uncontrolled growth is **cancer**.
teach.mnemonic: SAME BOOK, DIFFERENT PAGES OPEN. Cells differ by which GENES are ON — not by different DNA.
teach.poweredIdea: Cells share identical DNA but differentiate by expressing different genes; lost cell-cycle control causes cancer.

data.prompt: Cells in one organism become specialized by turning on different _____.
data.hint: Same DNA, but different ones are switched on

data.paragraph: Among birds, skin cells that grow feathers must contain different DNA than the skin cells that grow scales.
data.bugPhrase: must contain different DNA than the skin cells that grow scales
data.hint: Do specialized cells in one body actually carry different DNA?
data.canonicalFix: All of the bird's cells share the same DNA. Feather-growing and scale-growing cells differ because they express different genes, not because their DNA is different.
data.poweredIdea: Specialized cells share identical DNA; they differ by which genes they express.

data.story: A cell's cell-cycle control genes are damaged, and the cell begins dividing nonstop, forming a growing mass of cells.
data.question: What does this situation best illustrate?
data.answer: Cancer — a loss of control over the cell cycle leading to uncontrolled division
options: Cancer — a loss of control over the cell cycle leading to uncontrolled division
Normal differentiation into a specialized tissue
A cell that has stopped dividing entirely
A cell switching from mitosis to meiosis
data.explanation: When cell-cycle regulation is lost, cells divide uncontrollably — the defining feature of cancer.

data.correct: Expressing different genes from the same DNA
distractors: Each cell type carrying different DNA
Cells losing their DNA over time

achievement.flavor: You explain specialization as different genes switched on — and cancer as lost cell-cycle control.
